note: Nine atoms. serves_concepts reflects vault row attachment per Catalog build-status.

strategies.label: Greet Students at the Door
strategies.summary: Greeting students at the door is one example of an effective entry routine. The goal is not the greeting itself; the goal is creating a predictable transition from the hallway into learning.
solves: Unstructured transition time
Difficulty beginning class
Limited teacher-student connection
Lost instructional minutes
Lack of predictability
mechanism: Predictable routines reduce uncertainty — cognitive load drops
Students receive an immediate cue that learning has begun — attention shifts in
Teachers gather quick information before instruction
Positive interactions strengthen relationships and belonging
Entry becomes intentional rather than accidental
conditions: Students know what to do immediately after entering — routine taught
Bell work or an opening task is already prepared
Materials are accessible
Classroom expectations have been explicitly taught
Teacher can monitor both hallway and classroom

misconception.common: Standing at the door is often presented as best practice.
misconception.principle: Create a predictable, personal transition into learning.

implementations.label: Relational
implementations.description: Teacher greets every student by name and briefly checks in before directing them to the opening task.
best_fit: Teachers who enjoy conversation
Smaller classes

implementations.label: Procedural
implementations.description: Teacher greets students while directing them to begin a posted bell ringer.
best_fit: Teachers emphasizing efficient transitions
Larger classes

implementations.label: Low-Verbal
implementations.description: Teacher stands near the entrance, makes eye contact, smiles or nods, while students independently begin the entry routine.
best_fit: Teachers with quieter personalities
Students who thrive on predictable routines

adaptations: Morning meeting
Advisory
Secondary block schedule
Kindergarten welcome song
Student greeters
Digital check-in
Mood meter
Visual check-in
strategies.evidence_note: Cook et al. (2018) found positive greetings raised academic engagement ~20 percentage points and reduced disruptive behavior ~9 points. Scope: individual, personal greetings — not any warm gesture.
sol_connections: Predictability
Attention
Cognitive Load
Retrieval through Routine

strategies.label: Restorative Interactions
strategies.summary: 2×10 is two minutes of non-academic conversation with one hard-to-reach student, held for ten school days running. The goal is not the ten conversations themselves; the goal is building a durable relationship with a student who is currently reachable only through the deed, not the person. Attributed to Raymond Wlodkowski; later popularized in Allen Mendler's Connecting with Students.
solves: A student who feels unseen or only-seen-when-in-trouble
Redirections that keep spending the bond instead of building it
A relationship that starts and stays in the negative
Escalating behavior with no relational channel to reach through
Limited one-on-one connection during a full teaching day
mechanism: Ten consecutive days signals reliability — the student learns the adult keeps coming back
Non-academic content means the interaction is not about compliance
Repeated positive contact builds relationship before the next hard moment
A felt sense of belonging conditions motivation
The channel engagement and feedback travel on gets stronger
conditions: The conversations stay genuinely non-academic — no schoolwork, no behavior talk
The teacher can protect two low-stakes minutes daily
Consistency across all ten days — a broken streak resets the signal
The teacher is curious about this student, not gathering leverage
The student is not put on the spot publicly

misconception.common: 2x10 is often presented as a behavior-fix trick.
misconception.principle: Build the relationship before you need it, on the student's terms, not the classroom's.

implementations.label: Conversational
implementations.description: Teacher initiates a brief, genuine chat about the student's interests — a game, a show, a weekend — following the student's lead each day.
best_fit: Teachers who connect easily through talk
Students who warm to verbal attention

implementations.label: Low-Verbal
implementations.description: Teacher uses short, repeated micro-contacts: noticing a shirt, a quick shared joke, a saved seat. Two minutes spread across small moments rather than one sit-down.
best_fit: Teachers with quieter styles
Students who find direct one-on-one talk intense

implementations.label: Interest-Anchored
implementations.description: Teacher opens with something from an interest survey or an observed hobby, and returns to that thread daily so the student sees continuity from one day to the next.
best_fit: Teachers who prefer a concrete starting point
Students who take time to trust that attention is real

adaptations: Split the two minutes across two staff who share the student
Advisory or homeroom slot
Written back-and-forth for students who prefer text to talk
Interest survey as a launch point
Extend past ten days when momentum is building
Team version: several teachers each run 2x10 with different students
Elementary morning check-in
Secondary hallway or transition contact
strategies.evidence_note: Wlodkowski's 85% improvement figure is practitioner-reported and illustrative, not a measured finding.
sol_connections: Belonging conditions motivation
Feedback received through relationship (SoL Q2/Q4)
rp_connections: Relationship built before trouble is what lets correction land later
Naming the deed not the doer

strategies.label: Co-Created Norms
strategies.summary: Co-created norms are a class agreement authored with students. The goal is not the list on the wall; the goal is authorship. Students who help write the norms hold them, because they own them. This is where investment replaces compliance.
solves: Expectations that students follow but do not believe
Rules that feel imposed rather than shared
Weak buy-in when a teacher hands down a posted list
Norms that get ignored the moment the teacher looks away
A thin sense of belonging in the room's culture
mechanism: Authorship creates ownership — students hold norms they helped write
Investment replaces compliance: the agreement is theirs, so following it is self-consistency rather than obedience
Autonomy of authorship feeds motivation — voice in the rules raises the will to keep them (SoL Q4)
Shared, predictable expectations reduce extraneous cognitive load — students are not guessing what is allowed
Co-authorship is a pathway to belonging — helping name how the room treats each other is a way of belonging to it
conditions: Student voice is real, not decorative — their words actually make it onto the wall
Norms are few, simple, and positively stated
The agreement is revisited and revised, not signed once and forgotten
Enough relational trust exists that students will speak honestly
The teacher is willing to be bound by the agreement too

misconception.common: Let the students make the rules is often presented as the practice.
misconception.principle: Authorship creates ownership — students hold the norms they helped write.

implementations.label: K-2: Read-Aloud to Values
implementations.description: Teacher reads a picture book about friendship or fairness, then asks how the class wants the room to feel. Student answers become a short anchor chart, illustrated and signed.
best_fit: Early elementary
Teachers who anchor culture in story and image

implementations.label: Upper Elementary: Co-Drafted Agreement
implementations.description: Students brainstorm in small groups, the class clusters ideas into shared expectations, and everyone drafts and signs the agreement. Posted and revisited regularly.
best_fit: Grades 3-5
Teachers who want a durable, student-owned document

implementations.label: Middle School: Discussion of Why
implementations.description: Before writing anything, students discuss why norms matter — what a good room feels like, what erodes it. From that conversation they co-create and commit to the agreement.
best_fit: Grades 6-8
Teachers building motivation through reasoning and voice

adaptations: Advisory or morning meeting norm-setting
Group-work agreements for a single project
Digital collaborative draft
Norm revisit after a rough week
Student-facilitated norm review
Restorative circle to author or renew the agreement
Family or home input into the class values
strategies.evidence_note: No head-to-head study of co-created vs. teacher-set norms exists. Grounded in autonomy mechanisms (SoL Q4) and belonging-through-co-authorship (Klevan 2021). The effect is on investment, not necessarily rule-following frequency.
sol_connections: Autonomy of authorship feeds Motivation (SoL Q4)
Predictable expectations reduce extraneous Cognitive Load
Working Memory freed for learning when the room is predictable
rp_connections: Co-created norms shift compliance to investment (Klevan 2021)

strategies.label: Teach the Transition
strategies.summary: A transition is taught and rehearsed the way content is taught — modeled, practiced, and named — rather than announced once and enforced afterward. The goal is not a quiet move between activities; the goal is a sequence students can run without holding it in their heads.
solves: The seam between activities is where most instructional time leaks
Students stall at the boundary not because they're refusing but because they don't know the next action
The teacher ends up narrating every move, which makes the class dependent on the narration
Noise and drift at the seam get read as a behavior tension when the source is structural
mechanism: A rehearsed sequence runs from memory rather than being assembled on the spot — working memory is freed for the work waiting on the other side of the move
Each rehearsal is a low-stakes retrieval of the sequence, which strengthens it — spaced and retrieval-based practice makes it durable
A known sequence narrows what attention has to track — one next action instead of a whole noisy room
Teaching the move in advance means the teacher shapes the moment rather than correcting after it
When students help build the sequence, they move through a structure they hold rather than one imposed on them
conditions: The steps are few and concrete enough to rehearse
There is time set aside to practice it early, before it's needed under pressure
The signal is consistent — a cue that changes weekly has to be re-learned each time
The room supports it — materials where hands already are, a visible next step
The sequence gets re-rehearsed after breaks and when it degrades

misconception.common: Often presented as getting students to move quickly and quietly.
misconception.principle: Students can only run a sequence they've practiced. Anything not rehearsed has to be assembled in the moment, and the moment is when there's least room to assemble it.

implementations.label: Rehearsed and named
implementations.description: Walk the sequence with students when nothing is happening: name the steps, model it, run it two or three times, name what made it work.
best_fit: Early elementary
Any group meeting a new format

implementations.label: Student-built
implementations.description: Students draft the sequence themselves — what should this look like, what gets in the way, what's our signal — then rehearse their own version.
best_fit: Upper elementary and middle
Any room where compliance is the current sticking point

implementations.label: Role-carried
implementations.description: Specific students carry the transition: caller, materials lead, timekeeper. The sequence travels through roles rather than through the teacher's voice.
best_fit: Students who struggle most at the seam — the role gives the regulation something to attach to

adaptations: K–2: attach the sequence to a song, chant, or counted signal; pair it with a picture schedule
3–5: students manage their own materials inside the sequence; introduce a visible timer
6–8: fewer steps, stated once, then handed over; students set the norm for what a clean move looks like
After a disruption — sub, assembly, testing week — rehearse rather than assume; the sequence degrades
strategies.evidence_note: Kounin (1970) established momentum and smoothness — well-managed classrooms anticipate friction at activity boundaries rather than reacting to it.
sol_connections: Automaticity frees working memory (SoL Q1)
Spaced retrieval-based practice makes sequences durable
Verbal + visual representation outperforms either alone
rp_connections: Predictable, co-held routines lower the need for correction (Klevan 2021)

strategies.label: The Repair Conversation
strategies.summary: A short, structured conversation after harm, built on four questions that surface what happened and what would make it right — held with each person separately first, then together when both are ready. The goal is not an apology; the goal is that the student stays inside the community that has to keep working after the incident.
solves: Something happened and the room can't just proceed as if it didn't
The available responses feel like a choice between letting it go and removing someone
A forced apology gets produced and nothing about tomorrow is different
The student who caused harm leaves knowing they're in trouble but not what they'd do differently
mechanism: Who does the accounting: in a consequence the adult names the wrong; in a repair conversation the student constructs the account — that's the part that changes behavior
'What happened?' opens a story; 'Why did you do that?' invites a defense — the wording is doing the work
Naming who was affected makes the harm concrete and external
The student stays inside relationships and belonging, which is the channel any future correction has to travel through
The encounter itself generates the solidarity the agreement rests on (Why RJ Works, 2021)
conditions: Relationship is already banked
Both people are regulated enough to talk
Each person is met separately first
The teacher can sit with silence and not fill it
The agreement reached is small enough to actually happen and gets followed up on

misconception.common: Often presented as the soft alternative to a consequence.
misconception.principle: Harm is the problem to be addressed, not the person. The response has to keep the student inside the community that has to metabolize what happened.

implementations.label: The four questions
implementations.description: What happened? What were you thinking at the time? Who was affected, and how? What would make it right? Then the same four with the other person, then together.
best_fit: The standard case — two students, a clear incident, both able to talk

implementations.label: Separate-then-together (mediated)
implementations.description: Teacher works with each student individually first, building perspective-taking before either has to face the other.
best_fit: Conflicts with real heat
Where one student is much more verbal than the other

implementations.label: Low-verbal / written
implementations.description: Same four questions on paper or drawn, or answered one at a time across a day rather than in one sitting.
best_fit: Students who shut down under face-to-face questioning
Anyone who needs processing time

adaptations: K–2: two questions, not four — what happened and what would help. Concrete restitution the child can physically do.
3–5: all four questions, teacher-facilitated. Introduce the apology-of-action.
6–8: students can facilitate for peers. Privacy matters most at this age.
Teacher-and-student repair: the same four questions when the rupture is between you and a student. This is the version teachers skip and the one students remember.
strategies.evidence_note: Exclusionary discipline is associated with increased future misbehavior and dropout risk (Klevan 2021). Strongest caution: fidelity, not efficacy — a conversation run once after a blowup is not the same intervention as a practice running all year.
sol_connections: Feedback received through the relationship (SoL Q2)
Belonging conditions motivation (SoL Q4)
rp_connections: Harm met by restoring the relationship and preserving community (Klevan 2021)
Why RJ Works (2021) — mechanism is the encounter itself

strategies.label: Design the Room Around the Work
aliases: Design the Room Around the Work
strategies.summary: Arrange furniture, materials, and traffic paths around what students actually do in the room — where hands work, where bodies move, what has to be seen. The goal is not a tidy room; the goal is that the easiest physical action is also the one the lesson needs.
solves: Minutes disappear into retrieving, distributing, and returning materials
The same two spots generate friction every day and it reads as behavior
Moving between formats takes long enough that teachers stop doing it
Students can't reach materials without crossing the room or disturbing others
mechanism: Friction reduced at the point of action — a student whose materials are where their hands already are doesn't have to cross the room or interrupt the work
Traffic flow designed in advance means the room itself guides behavior without narration
Transitions between formats (desks → circle → groups) are faster when the room is built for the moves the day requires
Physical arrangement sets cognitive conditions — a room that enables the work is a room where learning load stays on the learning
conditions: The room is arranged before students arrive, not improvised in the moment
Materials live at the point of use, not in a central storage spot that requires a trip
Traffic paths are tested — the teacher walks the most common routes before students do
The arrangement anticipates the full range of formats the day will use

misconception.common: Room design is often treated as an aesthetic choice or a one-time setup.
misconception.principle: The room is infrastructure. Its arrangement either enables the work or competes with it.

implementations.label: Materials at the point of use
implementations.description: Station materials at each table or group rather than at a central location. Students retrieve and return within their own area.
best_fit: Any room with frequent small-group work

implementations.label: Traffic path design
implementations.description: Map the three most common routes in the room and clear them of friction points before the year starts.
best_fit: Rooms where student movement is frequent

implementations.label: Format-based arrangement
implementations.description: Set up for the first format of the day and stage the next format's materials so transitions between them take under two minutes.
best_fit: Secondary block schedules
Elementary classrooms with multiple instructional formats

adaptations: K–2: low shelves labeled with pictures; materials in baskets at each table; a clear visual path to the meeting area
3–5: student jobs include materials setup and return; groups know their supply location
6–8: arrangements shift by unit rather than day; students help configure the room for a new format
sol_connections: Physical environment as cognitive scaffold — external structure reduces load on working memory
Reducing extraneous friction preserves attention for the work
rp_connections: Room design that enables movement without surveillance supports student agency

strategies.label: Post What You'd Otherwise Repeat
strategies.summary: Make visible the information students would otherwise have to hold in their heads or ask you for — the sequence, the schedule, the steps, the criteria. The goal is not a decorated wall; the goal is that the room carries the information so working memory doesn't have to.
solves: The same question gets asked five times an hour about something already said
Students who missed the verbal instruction have no way to recover it except asking
A multi-step task stalls halfway because the middle steps have fallen out of memory
Transitions require the teacher to narrate what's next, every time
mechanism: A posted sequence is external memory — the steps are read rather than recalled, which returns working memory to the actual task (SoL Q1)
Information presented both visually and verbally is better supported than either alone
A visible schedule activates prior knowledge and makes the day anticipatable, which frees attention rather than spending it on uncertainty
Predictability is a safety condition — a student who can see what's coming isn't managing threat, and a student who lost the thread can recover without a public admission
conditions: The posted information is current — an outdated schedule is worse than none
The visual is at student eye level and in a consistent location
Students have been shown how to use it, not just that it exists
What's posted matches what the teacher says — contradictions breed uncertainty

misconception.common: Posted displays are often treated as decoration or compliance signals.
misconception.principle: Post what you'd otherwise have to repeat. If you'd say it again anyway, it belongs on the wall.

implementations.label: The daily schedule
implementations.description: Post the sequence of the day in a fixed location. Update it before students arrive. Students check it rather than ask.
best_fit: Elementary classrooms
Any room where the daily structure isn't self-evident

implementations.label: The task anchor chart
implementations.description: Before releasing students to work, post the steps of the task. Leave it up while they work.
best_fit: Multi-step tasks
Independent work periods where the teacher circulates

implementations.label: The rubric or criteria
implementations.description: Post success criteria before the work starts and leave them visible during revision. Students self-assess against a shared reference rather than against the teacher's judgment.
best_fit: Writing or project-based work
Any context where quality is the target

adaptations: K–2: picture-based schedules alongside words; icons on anchor charts; the posted sequence matched to the song or chant used to teach it
3–5: students maintain the task chart as a job; posted criteria become a self-check before turning in
6–8: criteria posted as student-generated success markers; the teacher replaces the daily schedule with a period agenda students can see on entry
sol_connections: External memory reduces working memory load (SoL Q1)
Dual-channel representation (visual + verbal) supports learning better than either alone
Activating prior knowledge via visible schedule prepares attention
rp_connections: Predictability as a belonging mechanism — a student who knows what's coming is not managing uncertainty

strategies.label: Third Point Feedback
strategies.summary: Aim the feedback at a shared external reference — a rubric, a model, the criteria, the work itself — rather than at the student. Teacher and student sit on the same side looking at a third thing. The goal is not softer criticism; the goal is that the student can evaluate the work without defending themselves.
solves: Accurate feedback gets rejected — the student hears a judgment about them and stops listening
A conference turns into reassurance because the honest version would feel like an attack
Students can't tell the difference between 'this draft isn't there yet' and 'you aren't good at this'
Revision doesn't happen because accepting the feedback would mean accepting the verdict that came with it
mechanism: Ego-threat feedback is rejected regardless of accuracy — being right isn't sufficient; the feedback has to be receivable (SoL Q2)
Feedback travels on relationships — the same words land as help or as threat depending on what's already between teacher and student
The third point gives the student goal, current position, and next step — the three things effective feedback supplies (Hattie & Timperley, 2007)
Same structure as naming the deed, not the doer — the person stays separable from what's being evaluated
conditions: The third point exists and is visible — a rubric the student helped write, a model worth comparing to, the actual criteria
The feedback names the gap between the work and the reference, not between the student and your expectations
The student has enough relationship with the teacher that the conversation is safe to have
Time exists for the student to act on it — feedback without a revision opportunity is informational at best

misconception.common: Third point is often heard as 'be nicer' or 'don't criticize directly.'
misconception.principle: The point is not to soften the feedback. It's to redirect where the student's attention is during the exchange — away from their standing and toward the work.

implementations.label: Rubric-anchored conference
implementations.description: Place the rubric between you and the student. Point to specific criteria. 'Here's where the work is; here's where the criteria put it.'
best_fit: Writing conferences
Project review

implementations.label: Model comparison
implementations.description: Place a strong example alongside the student's work. Ask the student to name what's different. The student does the comparison.
best_fit: Any task with a clear quality bar
Students who shut down under direct feedback

implementations.label: Self-assessment first
implementations.description: Student rates the work against the criteria before the teacher does. Conference begins with 'where do you think it is?' rather than the teacher's verdict.
best_fit: Upper elementary and middle
Any room building toward independent revision

adaptations: K–2: the 'third point' is a physical exemplar or drawing — 'this one is all the way done; what does yours still need?'
3–5: student-generated criteria make the third point something they own before the feedback starts
6–8: peer feedback structured around a shared rubric is third-point feedback without the teacher as the source
strategies.evidence_note: Hattie & Timperley (2007) identified three elements of effective feedback: goal, current position, next step. SoL Q2 (Deans for Impact, 2026): ego-threat feedback is rejected regardless of accuracy.
sol_connections: Ego-threat feedback rejected regardless of accuracy (SoL Q2)
Feedback effective when it specifies goal, current position, next step (Hattie & Timperley)
rp_connections: Naming the deed not the doer — the person stays separable from what's being evaluated

strategies.label: Everybody Answers
strategies.summary: Structure the question so every student produces an answer — on paper, to a partner, with a signal — before anyone shares aloud. The goal is not more hands up; the goal is that every student has actually retrieved something, because retrieval is where the learning happens and a raised hand only tells you about the one person raising it.
solves: The same four students answer everything, and the room reads as engaged because they are
You can't tell who's with you — quiet is doing double duty as thinking and checked out
A student who's lost has no low-risk way to try, so they wait it out
The lesson runs on the student most willing to talk, not on whether the class has the concept
mechanism: Every student retrieves — the learning is in the retrieval, not in the answer given aloud (SoL Q1/Q2)
Writing or signaling before sharing gives processing time to students who need it, which is a competence condition for belonging — you belong in a room where you can participate
The teacher gets information about the whole class, not just the hand-raisers
Low-risk formats (whiteboards, written, partner) lower the stakes of being wrong, which is a prerequisite for trying
conditions: The format is genuinely low-risk — partner answers, written responses, whiteboards that face down until the signal
The question is worth thinking about — Everybody Answers on a recall question produces compliance, not retrieval
Answers aren't graded or judged in the moment — the point is that everyone tries, not that everyone is right
The move is used often enough that it's expected, so students aren't performing for a novel format

misconception.common: Often presented as an engagement management technique, grounded in response rate.
misconception.principle: The mechanism is retrieval practice, not participation frequency. A student who produces an answer — even a wrong one — has done the cognitive work that changes what they remember. A student who watches someone else answer hasn't.

implementations.label: Think-write-share
implementations.description: Pose the question. Students write an answer. Then pairs share. Then the class discusses. The writing step is non-optional.
best_fit: Any question worth thinking about
Classes where verbal confidence varies widely

implementations.label: Whiteboard / signal response
implementations.description: Students write on mini-whiteboards or hold up a card and show at a signal. Teacher scans the room rather than calling on one student.
best_fit: Checks for understanding
Factual retrieval
Rooms where quick feedback matters

implementations.label: Partner-then-group
implementations.description: Every student answers to a partner first; then pairs share with a group; then groups share with the class. The answer is already formed before it reaches public air.
best_fit: Complex questions
Any room where public risk is high

adaptations: K–2: thumbs up/thumbs down, stands up/sits down, or a picture card — every student responds physically before the answer comes out
3–5: response cards, partner-writes, quick-writes — the written step is the retrieval
6–8: the written step matters more, not less — adolescents are more risk-averse publicly; the pre-write or partner step is the condition that makes participation safe
strategies.evidence_note: Grounded in retrieval practice (SoL Q1/Q2 — Deans for Impact, 2026) and competence-before-buy-in. Not grounded in response rate or Opportunities to Respond (OTR) literature. The OTR framing optimizes for frequency and produces fast shallow questioning, which is the opposite of this move.
sol_connections: Retrieval practice strengthens memory — every student retrieving is the mechanism (SoL Q1/Q2)
Processing time before sharing is a competence condition
rp_connections: Belonging requires the ability to participate — low-risk formats are a belonging mechanism, not just an engagement one
